### Introduction to IApplicationThread
[`IApplicationThread`](https://cs.android.com/android/platform/superproject/+/android-16.0.0_r1:frameworks/base/core/java/android/app/IApplicationThread.aidl) is a private callback provided to system from apps so that system can use it to send commands (load specified app, notify changes of component lifecycle, etc) to app

It is intended to only usable from system, [so there are no permission checks](https://cs.android.com/android/platform/superproject/+/android-16.0.0_r1:frameworks/base/core/java/android/app/ActivityThread.java;l=1143), and security is guaranteed solely by the fact that the object is not obtained by a malicious process. This sounds somewhat similar to the concept of "cookies" or "tokens" in web. Such access control model is called as [Capability-based Security](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capability-based_security)

I previously discussed what attackers can do with it in [my blog](https://blog.canyie.top/2026/06/09/android-security-tricks/#%E5%A6%82%E4%BD%95%E5%88%A9%E7%94%A8-IApplicationThread). Simply put, if someone else managed to obtain an `IApplicationThread` from other processes, they can send arbitrary commands and the victim app would just process the fabricated commands like they were generated by system. In [a previous exploit of CVE-2022-20452](https://github.com/michalbednarski/LeakValue) (btw, personally I strongly suggest you read that brilliant exploit and writeup written by Michal Bednarski, his extensive work greatly inspired me) the trick was used to perform arbitrary code execution

### RemoteTransition
While `IApplicationThread` should only be passed to system process, it can be unexpectedly sent out of system_server

No one would implement an `getIApplicationThreadForApp(String packageName)` API that is exposed to any one, it is an obvious security violation

But if `IApplicationThread` is wrapped in another object and the outer wrapper object gets sent, it is a more likely scenario

[`RemoteTransition`](https://cs.android.com/android/platform/superproject/+/android-16.0.0_r1:frameworks/base/core/java/android/window/RemoteTransition.java;l=36;bpv=0) is such a wrapper which contains an `IApplicationThread` in order to boost priority of app that is running an animation

One user of that API is Launcher3, the default home application on AOSP and Pixel devices, which [creates an ActivityOptions using a RemoteTransition](https://cs.android.com/android/platform/superproject/+/android-16.0.0_r1:packages/apps/Launcher3/quickstep/src/com/android/launcher3/QuickstepTransitionManager.java;l=358) and then pass it to `startActivity()`

While Launcher3 itself does not expose the object to untrusted factors, the system_server sometimes does

[CVE-2022-20419](https://android.googlesource.com/platform/frameworks/base/+/e5dd8be748c76c11615050c610dfc1fae73ad4a4) occurred because system_server forwarded caller-passed `ActivityOptions` to launched app but forgot to strip `RemoteTransition`, allowing launched app to receive it and load arbitrary code inside launcher process

### TransitionPlayer
During shared-element transition animation, a lot of work has to done and communications need to happen between `WMCore` and `WMShell`, where `WM` means `Window Manager`

You can read [this article](https://cs.android.com/android/platform/superproject/+/android-16.0.0_r1:frameworks/base/libs/WindowManager/Shell/src/com/android/wm/shell/docs/overview.md) to understand `WMShell`

As `WMCore` and `WMShell` runs in different processes (`WMCore` runs in system_server and `WMShell` runs in SystemUI), they utilize the Binder mechanism to talk with each other

`WMCore` exposed a Binder [`registerTransitionPlayer` API](https://cs.android.com/android/platform/superproject/+/android-16.0.0_r1:frameworks/base/core/java/android/window/IWindowOrganizerController.aidl;l=88) and [`WMShell` uses it to register its own binder](https://cs.android.com/android/platform/superproject/+/android-16.0.0_r1:frameworks/base/libs/WindowManager/Shell/src/com/android/wm/shell/transition/Transitions.java;l=396)

When animation is started, `WMCore` calls `requestStartTransition` and [`TransitionRequestInfo`](https://cs.android.com/android/platform/superproject/+/android-16.0.0_r1:frameworks/base/core/java/android/window/TransitionRequestInfo.java;l=53;bpv=0) is passed to remote, [which includes the initial RemoteTransition](https://cs.

# Root My Galaxy SM-S9180 (dm3q) S9180ZCS8FZG1 — China (CHC) Payload Port

Port of the CVE-2026-43499 payload (UAF → KernelSU LKM temporary root) for
**Samsung Galaxy S23 Ultra SM-S9180 (dm3q)** running the **China (CHC)** firmware
**S9180ZCS8FZG1** (build 3251900).

- Kernel: `5.15.189-android13-8-3251900-abS9180ZCS8FZG1`
- Root method: CVE-2026-43499 UAF exploit + KernelSU LKM (temporary root, lost on reboot)
- Status: **working** — exploit succeeds on the first attempt; `su -c id` → `uid=0(root) context=u:r:ksu:s0`
- Verified alongside: Chinese negative screen (三星智慧主页) + Google GMS (Play Services 26.32.34 / Play Store / GSF) coexist on the same ROM.

## Files

| File | Description |
|---|---|
| `RootMyGalaxy-S9180-CHC.apk` | Signed APK (v3, CN=RMG), installable, contains the CHC payload |
| `cve-2026-43499-chc-app.so` | Patched CHC payload, md5 `5292cdf88e64cf54bd1b4b44f63e45ed` |
| `chc-patch-spec.json` | 10 movz patches applied to the working **TGY FZG1** payload |
| `chc-target.h` | CHC target profile with corrected offsets |

## Key finding — the CHC kallsyms trap

The CHC kallsyms table parses with an **off-by-one name shift**: every parsed
symbol name is attached to the address of the **next** symbol. Trusting the
naive parse produced wrong data-symbol addresses (v1–v4 failed at
`starting-temporary-root` or crashed). All addresses below were verified by
content checks, code-reference fingerprinting, and byte-identical windows
against the working TGY kernel — **do not re-derive them from the raw parse**:

| Symbol | Naive parse (WRONG) | Corrected |
|---|---|---|
| `init_task` | 0x02c06280 | **0x02c05080** |
| `root_task_group` | 0x02cb9cc0 | **0x02cb9ac0** |
| `selinux_state` (enforcing) | 0x02d8e648 | **0x02d8e5c0** |
| `system_unbound_wq` | 0x02a90808 | **0x02a90800** |
| `kmalloc_caches` | 0x02064a48 | **0x020648f8** |
| `anon_pipe_buf_ops` | 0x01e7f900 | **0x01e7f8e0** |
| `sysctl_bootid` (slide) | 0x02e6c0c4 | **0x02e6c0b1** |

Content-verified symbols that match TGY (already correct in the port):
`ashmem_fops` 0x0200d938, `ashmem_misc.fops` 0x02bfcf28,
`nfulnl_logger` 0x02a91e48, `random_table` 0x02bba8c0.
All code symbols are byte-identical to the TGY kernel (e.g.
`call_usermodehelper_exec_work` 0x001045d0).
